article_text:
“ Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom ” is launching into Italy as the opener of Lucca Comics and Games on the eve of Halloween, which, coincidentally, also happens to be when this third feature in the Aardman Animations’ hit stop-motion spinoff franchise is set.

Matthew Walker, who is the film’s co-director, is clearly pleased to be attending the 60th edition of this unique geek meet held within the 16th century walls of the medieval Tuscan town of Lucca because, as he puts is, “yeah, I am a geek myself.”

Related Stories

How to Watch MLB World Series 2026: Tampa Bay Rays vs. Milwaukee Brewers Online for Free

Fox and Endemol Shine Team to Adapt 'Fear Factor' as a Scripted Microdrama Series for My Drama App

Unsurprisingly, when he meets the Italian press in Lucca, the first question is about whether this new “Shaun the Sheep” entry, famously handmade frame by frame with clay puppets, can be seen as a symbolic bastion against the encroaching spread of AI through filmmaking and the myriad concerns this is raising.

Walker subsequently sat with Variety and drilled down on why he thinks AI-made animation is not an existential threat for Aardman. At least not for the moment. And why animation films may be more immune to the impact of AI than live action ones.

Something I love about stop-motion is the tactile physicality of it and I think that’s what appeals to audiences. You obviously want to tell a funny emotional story with these characters. But on top of that, I think that just the technique of it, the stop motion technique, has a lot of appeal in the knowledge that these are real models all built with incredible detail by the artists. When Aardman release behind-the-scenes footage videos, they are always really popular because people love seeing how stop-motion is made. People really respond to seeing these huge detailed sets with these little puppets, which is obviously something AI can’t replicate. I also think there is a desire for imperfection. We’ve gotten to a point now with digital technology where we can kind of do anything; things can be so beautifully polished. So there’s a desire to kind of step back and bring back some imperfection. You see it in things like [Sony Pictures Animation] “Spider-Verse” franchise, where they’re introducing the 2D element and even hand-drawn pencil lines and stuff. It’s because there’s a desire to see the craft behind the finished product. Like being able to see the pencil lines. In stop motion, it’s about being able to see the fingerprints.

Yes. At the moment it certainly feels like that’s the case. I know AI is advancing all the time, and we might get to a point where it’s really difficult to tell the difference. But I think at the moment, even when they might not be able to identify what’s not right, I think the audience can kind of tell when something is made with AI because there’s something a little bit uncanny. Something that doesn’t quite feel right. When something is artificial you can tell, even though you can’t necessarily articulate why. AI can replicate art, but I don’t think it can replicate the emotion and reason behind the art. It doesn’t necessarily understand why those pencil lines were made. Whereas I think a human audience recognizes the craftsmanship that goes into something.

Yes, I think so. With stop motion and the work that Aardman does it’s very much about the characters and the performances of those characters. It’s similar to when you watch a live-action film. You know, with a good actor, you really respond to the emotional performance. And it’s the same with an animated character. The animator puts their own emotions into it. They’re essentially actors themselves, just doing it much more slowly than in live action. I think when you’re watching things from an early age, that becomes part of your knowledge of art and how you respond to it. And you take with you as you grow up.

I think animation is. A good animator can turn any object into a character. It’s like the Pixar lamp. it’s just a lamp. It has no face. It has no features. Has no limbs. But the way it’s animated, the way the animators have made it move, allows the audience to have an emotional connection with it. To see it as a character, as a sentient being. And that’s not replicating anything. With live action, by using AI it’s easier to replicate human activity because there’s a vast wealth of footage that AI is fed with. But in animation there isn’t that wealth of footage to work with, because the animation process starts entirely from scratch. If you take a ball or a lamp and give it life, that’s not based on anything. It’s just based on an understanding of what a human can connect with.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

article_text:
Solamente nel febbraio del 2025 MoMA e M+ avevano costruito un ponte di alleanza museale tra USA e Cina ; si aggiunge oggi anche Parigi, con un accordo che punta a ridefinire le modalità di collaborazione tra grandi istituzioni culturali. Il Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) di New York , il Centre Pompidou di Parigi e M+ di Hong Kong hanno infatti annunciato una nuova alleanza internazionale, sottoscrivendo un accordo quadro il 30 ottobre 2026 negli spazi del museo asiatico. L’intesa, che prevede la condivisione delle rispettive collezioni attraverso prestiti a lungo termine, la realizzazione di mostre sviluppate congiuntamente e programmi comuni di ricerca curatoriale e conservazione, mette in relazione tre istituzioni di riferimento per l’arte moderna e contemporanea con l’ambizione di ampliare la circolazione delle opere e favorire il confronto tra differenti prospettive culturali.

A firmare l’accordo sono stati i musei nelle persone di Christophe Cherix , Laurent Le Bon e Suhanya Raffel , rispettivamente David Rockefeller Director del MoMA, presidente del Centre Pompidou e direttrice di M+. Le tre istituzioni manterranno la propria identità e autonomia amministrativa, ma lavoreranno a una rete di collaborazione continuativa, mettendo in comune risorse, competenze e patrimoni. L’obiettivo è quello di costruire nuove occasioni di accesso alle opere e sviluppare modalità di lavoro condivise, superando una concezione della collezione museale come patrimonio circoscritto alla singola sede espositiva.

«Se avremo successo», ha dichiarato Le Bon alla testata ARTnews, durante un’intervista congiunta a cui hanno partecipato anche Raffel e Cherix, «saremo più della somma delle nostre parti, e credo che questo sia qualcosa di assolutamente nuovo».

Tre istituzioni, tre continenti

Fondate in momenti diversi del Novecento e del nuovo millennio, le tre istituzioni rappresentano altrettanti punti di riferimento per la storia e la diffusione della cultura visiva. Il MoMA , inaugurato nel 1929 a New York, ha contribuito in modo determinante alla definizione del canone dell’arte contemporanea, attraverso una collezione che comprende pittura, scultura, fotografia, architettura, design, cinema e nuovi media. Il Centre Pompidou , aperto a Parigi nel 1977, ha invece introdotto un modello museale fondato sul dialogo tra discipline, riunendo sotto lo stesso tetto arti visive, architettura, design, cinema e musica. M+ , inaugurato nel 2021 nel distretto culturale di West Kowloon a Hong Kong, è una delle più importanti istituzioni internazionali dedicate alla cultura visiva del XX e XXI secolo, con particolare attenzione alle produzioni artistiche e culturali dell’Asia.

La combinazione delle collezioni comporterà un patrimonio complessivo condiviso pari a centinaia di migliaia di oggetti, non considerando anche i vastissimi archivi. Secondo le stime attuali, i musei registreranno complessivamente 10 milioni di visitatori in presenza e 125 milioni di visitatori online all’anno. Tra gli obiettivi dichiarati figura la volontà di ottimizzare le risorse e ridurre l’impatto ambientale delle attività museali.

I prestiti a lungo termine potrebbero inoltre consentire di limitare i trasporti ripetuti delle opere, sostituendo in alcuni casi le spedizioni organizzate per singole esposizioni con trasferimenti meno frequenti e permanenze più estese. Tema che assume una particolare rilevanza per il Centre Pompidou, la cui sede storica parigina è attualmente chiusa per un importante intervento di ristrutturazione e non riaprirà prima del 2030 .

Prestiti e mostre condivise

Un comitato direttivo congiunto, composto dai direttori delle istituzioni, dai responsabili dei dipartimenti e dai curatori coinvolti, avrà il compito di definire le priorità comuni in materia di mostre, prestiti, ricerca, conservazione e formazione professionale. Sono previsti incontri mensili e un appuntamento annuale in presenza, che si svolgerà a rotazione nelle tre città. Il primo incontro è atteso al MoMA nel novembre 2026.

Tra le prime modalità di collaborazione individuate figurano i prestiti di lunga durata, che consentiranno di mantenere alcune opere nelle sedi partner per periodi più estesi rispetto a quelli abitualmente previsti dalle singole mostre temporanee. A partire dalla fine del 2027, una selezione di opere provenienti dalla collezione di M+ sarà presentata nelle gallerie del MoMA a New York. Nel 2028, inoltre, il museo newyorkese ospiterà uno spazio dedicato al Centre Pompidou. Altri progetti analoghi sono in fase di elaborazione per le sedi di Hong Kong e Parigi.

La programmazione comprenderà anche una grande mostra collettiva – da sviluppare nell’arco dei prossimi cinque anni e destinata a essere presentata in tutte e tre le istituzioni – che coinvolgerà opere provenienti dai rispettivi patrimoni e si concentrerà sul significato della contemporaneità, interrogando le modalità attraverso cui la produzione artistica viene interpretata e storicizzata in contesti culturali differenti. Un altro ambito centrale sarà quello della ricerca: i curatori di M+ e del Centre Pompidou entreranno infatti a far parte di C-MAP (Contemporary and Modern Art Perspectives), il programma interdisciplinare avviato dal MoMA per promuovere lo studio dell’arte moderna e contemporanea attraverso prospettive internazionali.

Bed（1998）——一张未整理的床，周围地板上散落着物品，暗示着在那张床上连续数日未曾离开。从外表看，Emin 的装置与 Stettheimer 那些珍贵的装置截然相反。然而，Emin 作品最初的接受情况呼应了 Marsden Hartley 的某种无助感：“人们不知道该如何面对这件作品，因为它包含了普通女性生活经验的全貌。”[2] article_text:
Artist and writer Dineke Blom visited the exhibition Bitches Brew at the Bonnefanten museum (Maastricht, the Netherlands) and wrote an impassioned essay exploring the role of personal figuration and the extent to which it reveals the artist. ‘In Bitches Brew , Keetje Mans, Tanja Ritterbex, and Aline Thomassen put an unexpected spin on personal figuration. ‘I take a life as lived by a woman as my starting point for each of the three exhibitions. The three artists share a great deal of their own lives—both in conversations with one another and through figurative elements in their work. Surprisingly, that open, personal aspect actually convinced me that Thomassen, Ritterbex, and Mans are masters of the art of concealment. False trail, smokescreen, witches’ brew—it is all encapsulated in that intriguing group portrait accompanying the exhibition.’

‘ A figurative painting depicting Black persons does not represent Black persons any more truthfully than an abstract painting can .’ I find the quote among my notes, without name or date, and jotted down when I was researching abstract working Afro American artists from the 1960s and 1970s. ‘Would the quote’s thesis also apply to a figurative painting depicting women ?’ I wondered when I visited the exhibition Bitches Brew at the Bonnefanten museum. And what if the painting also appears autobiographical — would that make it an even truer reflection? A reflection of what, exactly? These are questions that the exhibition raises for me as a viewer.

Three artists, each with a separate show, are central to Bitches Brew , collected under that overarching title. All three are women, a fact that is relevant to my account. All three make figurative work, and I see the depiction and representation of women as a common thread in their work. ‘Woman’, ‘personal’ and ‘autobiographical’ can be a problematic combination because the work risks being reduced to a highly personal artistic expression. When, long ago, I studied the work of the artist Florine Stettheimer (USA, 1871–1944) I saw precisely that happen, in a laudatory review by Stettheimer’s colleague, contemporary and admirer Marsden Hartley. His inability to grasp her hyper-feminine figuration is evident in the words he used to characterize the work as an “ultra-lyrical expression of an ultra-feminine spirit,”thus effectively smothering it. [1] A more recent example is Tracey Emin’s installation My Bed (1998) — an unmade bed surrounded by objects on the floor that suggest a days-long uninterrupted stay in that bed. In outward appearance Emin’s installation is the antithesis of Stettheimer’s precious installations. However, the initial reception of Emin’s work echoed something of Marsden Hartley’s helplessness: “people didn’t know where to put themselves in relation to the work, because it included the full range of an ordinary woman’s life experience.” [2] By now, in the visual arts an ordinary woman’s life experience as such will not raise eybrows. Wikipedia rightly describes Stettheimer as ‘modernist painter, feminist, theatre designer, poet and salonnière.’

Keetje Mans, Tanja Ritterbex and Aline Thomassen give a surprising twist to personal figuration in Bitches Brew . I take a life as lived by a woman as my starting point for each of the three exhibitions. The three artists share a great deal of their own lives—both in conversations with one another and via figurative elements in their work. Surprisingly, that open, personal aspect actually convinced me that Thomassen, Ritterbex, and Mans are masters of the art of concealment. False trail, smokescreen, witches’ brew—it is all encapsulated in the intriguing group portrait that accompanies the exhibition.

Not that their work is hermetic or impenetrable; it presents different angles from which one can look at, contemplate and fantasize over the life of a woman and/or female artist. In that sense it transcends the personal experience of the artists, however autobiographical their work may appear. What role personal figuration plays and how transparent it makes an artist is, to my mind, the overarching question the exhibition raises. Any answer to this question strikes me as complex from the outset, if only because I immediately think of a remark made by artist Mark Bradford, who happens to make abstract work. His answer to the question posed to him whether abstraction protects him from transparency was: ‘No. I think I could lie better through figuration. I could lie better with more props.’ What then do I think of, when looking at Keetje Mans’, Tanja Ritterbex’ and Aline Thomassen’s work in Bitches Brew , other than of the artists as persons ? That is yet another question that came to my mind.

The title of Aline Thomassen ’s exhibition is I am You- You are Me . In an interview with Aline Thomassen on the occasion of her winning the Ouborg Prize, her interviewer argued that her work ‘is about women.’ Thomassens’s response was: ‘They never ask say that about work that depicts men. So it’s about what those men and women do, what they express. It is about the content: struggle, internal struggle, etc., feelings that hopefully are universal, but they are presented by a woman.”[4] What Thomassen says here I see reflected in her section of the exhibition. The large back room shows a long horizontal row of depictions of women. They are naked, or rather they wear no clothes. For Thomassen clothes refer too much to the outside world, whereas she is interested in an ‘inner’ world. The body is what connects those two worlds.[5] In several of these images the bodies lay partly open and/or the watercolor painting dissolves into a proliferation of organs, umbilical cord, suggestions of plant forms, leaving the image battered.

I doubt that I am the only one who, at ‘naked’ and ‘being a woman’, thinks of what John Berger’s essay says about it being impossible for a woman to be truly naked as long as the eroticizing male gaze ‘dresses’ her naked body.[6] But there is no eroticizing gaze beneath the nudity that Thomassen paints. What strikes me about the long row of depictions are the faces, the look in the women’s eyes. Some meet your gaze and others look away. However intrusive, naked and open the depicted women may be, I do not get an insight into what goes on inside them, no glimpse of their inner world. That contrast makes me reflect on the relationship between being visible and not showing everything, between being naked and yet not making oneself transparent. The questioning (and/or averted) gaze of the women invites one to think bigger than the plight of a single individual woman, because what they represent concerns “the content: struggle, internal struggle, etc., feelings that hopefully are universal, but they are presented by a woman.” In this light the portraits invite me as a viewer to examine how this content stirs my own inner life, because I am You- You are Me .

The work of Tanja Ritterbex in her exhibition Mama Steht Kopf , is at first glance the most personal and autobiographical of the three artists. She always starts from her self-portrait and in interviews she comes across as ‘honest’ and direct; for example, there is hardly any time between a question and Ritterbex’s answer. But Ritterbex too, is a master of concealment. And however fast her answers may come, those answers are preceded by considerable reflection.

Her methodical working method is a case in point., The series of daily selfies (Selfie Series, 2015-2016) for example, ends at number 365, a rather impersonal breaking-off point: the number of days in a year. What follows is reflection on those selfies, for instance by posting them on social media, consider the responses, and then painting them — sometimes with acrylic paint because it can show more quickly than oil paint what image her thinking has produced. And here in Bitches Brew by making a selection from that series of small paintings.

In the accompanying video (Selfie Video, 2026) we see Ritterbex doing a minutes long dance in her studio. It is an intense and intimate image, with no audience. To me the video evoked instant happiness, because what I see is so liberating — as an artist you have your own biotope, your studio; that is your domain, there you are free. Yet for a fraction of a second it flashed through my head: ‘where is the hidden camera.’ But it really is Ritterbex who has placed the camera on herself. She explores an extremely personal moment so as to cast a meta gaze on her art. Ritterbex plays out ‘proximity’ and ‘distance’, just as I saw Thomassen do.

In a radio interview Ritterbex was asked about a painting: ‘You show yourself but also not. Which version of yourself do you show?’ Ritterbex answered: ‘The persona Ritterbex? Maybe I am now the mother character?’ The persona Ritterbex observes and questions the world. Those can be questions about motherhood, artistry, or about the fullness of life. Ritterbex was always told during her training that she ‘crammed everything’ into a painting; it was always ‘too full.’[7] Advice to make the image a bit less crammed she always set aside. What would she even omit, what should have been pushed further into the background so we get a full view of what is important ? Perhaps life itself is ‘full’ and you do not want to make that density transparent because you want to show that richness, that excess. So why not then put everything on that image, and with as little perspectival depth as possible because that would involuntarily steer you toward ‘in the foreground’ and ‘in the background’.

I see her refusal more as an existential choice than as a formal-aesthetic one. In the latter case her oeuvre would be a long line of cheerful carefree pictures offering a finished worldview. But not a single work is finished in that sense. Her paintings contain too many (conscious) loose ends; forms are ‘frayed’ and ‘provisional’. Ritterbex offers only the bare minimum to recognize a figure, a table, her daughter, her self-portrait, a small rug or towel. The multiplicity is not organized into an orderly whole. Of course Ritterbex makes choices in her paintings but regarding ‘fullness’ she pushes it to the limit. By driving it refers to what, exactly? to extremes, her paintings pose questions about the abundance of impressions from the world. That can be intimidating or appetizing. Precisely because Ritterbex shows the fullness I become aware of the underlying existential question. In this respect the work goes beyond the autobiographical. Ritterbex does not make herself transparent as a person. Instead, as an artist she creates space to raise a meaningful question, for example the question of how one copes with the abundance of impressions from the surrounding world, and how that translates into one’s work.

Bitches Brew begins with Keetje Mans ’ exhibition Shimmer of Bliss . In the first room works are displayed where the theme of “concealing” versus “giving openness” is most directly visible in both painting technique and figuration. Some paintings show suggestions of people with their faces hidden behind laundry on a clothesline or because the image is cropped exactly where you would expect the face atop a body (or is it a jug rather than a body?).

Also, in most paintings (details of) earlier figuration have disappeared beneath a thick layer of paint. Such spots I find intriguing. The artist Jack Whitten (USA 1939-2018) writes in his collected notes, referring to the paint-skin, that matter is ‘encoded information’ and the surface is thereby the ultimate carrier of content.[8] To me, Whitten’s view applies to Mans’ work.

Things I Want To Tell You (2023, oil on linnen) may illustrate my point. I saw this painting earlier in Stedelijk Museum Schiedam in the exhibition The roundness of loss (2025-2026). I stood before it for a long time and found it increasingly puzzling. The image is one big disappearing act. Paradoxically, the image as a whole stands like a house, which makes this ‘disappearing act’ pull me into the image even more. The Schiedam exhibition was about loss. Things I Want To Tell You depicts that, in my view — absence, withdrawn from sight; trying to retrieve a vanished image however much that image wants to disappear. And conversely, however much you try to bring it up, it recedes again.

The way the painting is constructed is a variant of the foreground versus background theme. Everything is actually in the foreground and that foreground is positioned two-dimensionally against a dark rear wall. Background here might be called under-ground in the sense that details that have been painted over now appear as signs of earlier detours, of other choices, roads not taken. Such spots remind me of the poem by Robert Frost:

The Road Not Taken

Two roads diverged in a yellow wood, And sorry I could not travel both And be one traveler, long I stood […] And both that morning equally lay In leaves no step had trodden black. Oh, I kept the first for another day! Yet knowing how way leads on to way,

I doubted if I should ever come back . […] [1915]

In Things I Want To Tell You the symbolism of extinguished light perhaps plays a role as well; see the little flames that have disappeared under the layer of paint. However, that kind of symbolism does not, in my experience, play a main role in this work. That role is reserved for the bright-white candelabrum with all those tentacle that fills up the image. The vitality of that radiant ornament is in your face. But at the same time the overpainted details underneath this same ornament evoke so much loss and ‘disappearing’ that vitality and visibility are increasingly felt as a provocation. For me this painting is the key to many of Mans’ other works.

To what extent does an artist make themselves.transparent with autobiographical elements in the work, and would the work — because of the personal figuration — be a reflection of ‘what it is to be a woman’? That was what I pondering while walking through the rooms. Keetje Mans, Tanja Ritterbex en Aline Thomassen show aspects of being-a-woman in their work and also use autobiographical elements. They make a life as lived by a woman palpable but they do not claim to show me or make me feel what being a woman is . At the same time they broaden their work, in which so many autobiographical elements can be recognized, beyond the sphere of highly personal experience. So no generalizations, and no reduction to the highly personal.

Bitches Brew , the exhibition’s title is, I presume, taken from the eponymous album by Miles Davis (1970). Wikipedia mentions that Davis sent his musicians into the studio with the instruction that they could play what they wanted, but on the basis of a simple chord scheme he gave them. The album had to be the result of improvisation, ‘Not some prearranged shit’. Just as the photo of Mans, Thomassen en Ritterbex with the three of them looking into the camera nudged me to a train of thought, so the exhibition title does something similar. Now to make me see the degree of improvisation in the exhibition as a whole. The underlying chord scheme, something in the spirit of ‘the life of a woman’, is implicit. I do not feel a constricting concept to the exhibition; rather I am invited to take part in a living exchange of ideas.

[4] Aline Thomassen in Kunstmuseum Den Haag, 2024. Fragment transcribed from YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B59TkmebfOw. [5] Aline Thomassen in Kunstmuseum Den Haag, 2024. Fragment transcribed from YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B59TkmebfOw. [6] John Berger, Ways of Seeing, chapter 3, Penguin Books 1972. [7] VPRO podcast Nooit meer slapen, 5 March 2026; Mister Motley-podcast Kunst is Lang, nr. 45 2017, Luuk Heezen. [8] Jack Whitten: Notes from the Woodshed, Hauser & Wirth Publishers, 2018, 2025; YouTube: School of Visual Arts Contemporary Perspectives Lecture with Jack Whitten: ‘Matter has the possibility of encoding information, and we can penetrate [into it to access that information]’.

—

article_text:
Für seine erste Soloschau in Rumänien hat sich der Künstler Christian Jankowski Hilfe von den mächtigsten Hexen des Landes geholt. Erkenntnis des Experiments: Magie sollte sich als kuratorische Praxis unbedingt durchsetzen

Zu einer vollkommen neuen und womöglich richtungsweisenden Präsentation von Kunst kommt es gerade in Bukarest. Im Kulturzentrum Scânteia+ zeigt der deutsche Künstler Christian Jankowski seine erste große Ausstellung in der rumänischen Hauptstadt, in der allein die Architektur enorm viele Geschichten zu erzählen hat. "The Promise" heißt die Schau. Welche Werke er dort präsentieren würde, entschied er nicht selbst. Er ließ sie durch eine Hexe und ihre Töchter auswählen.

Mihaela Minca heißt die Frau mit den magischen Kräften. Jankowski lernte sie über einen befreundeten Künstler kennen. Bei ihrem ersten Treffen wurde ein Schwein geschlachtet und gegessen. Etwa ein Jahr später legte der Künstler ihr Bilder seiner Performances, Videoarbeiten, Installationen und Skulpturen vor, und Minca "kuratierte" die Schau in einer bedachten Zeremonie.

Wer sich davon ein Bild machen möchte, hat dazu online Gelegenheit, denn der Privatsender Realitatea TV war nicht nur bei der Zauber-Session zugegen, er begleitete auch die Ausstellungseröffnung und strahlte sie live im Fernsehen aus. Das Ganze wurde wiederum Teil der Schau, die sowohl Retrospektive als auch eine Präsentation neuer Werke ist.

Sieh dir diesen Beitrag auf Instagram an Ein Beitrag geteilt von Vrajitoarea Mihaela Minca (@mihaelamincaofficial)

Die Ausstellung hat ihren Platz an einem der interessantesten Kunstorte der Stadt. Scânteia+ ist ein großer Raum mit fast acht Meter hohen Decken innerhalb der Casa Scânteii, der ehemaligen Druckerei des Presseorgans der Kommunistischen Partei Rumäniens. Ein Ort also, der viele Geschichten zu erzählen hat.

Als die Druckerpressen aus den Räumen befördert wurden, so erzählt es einer der Initiatoren des Kunstraums, seien große Löcher in die Wand gerissen worden. Die Pressen wurden dann vermutlich verschrottet, weil man noch etwas Geld mit dem Material machen konnte, sie wurden also nicht in ein Museum gebracht. In irgendeinem Flügel des Gebäudes werden heute noch TV-Formate produziert. Die Antennen auf dem Dach, die man auch von Weitem sieht, zeugen davon.

"It was once forgotten. It’s meant to be rediscovered. It is necessary" steht auf einem Poster im Treppenhaus. Im ersten dunklen Raum wird die Videoarbeit gezeigt, Ausschnitte aus der medialen Begleitung der Ausstellung durch den Privatsender, dahinter Jankowskis Skulpturen und neue Fotoarbeiten.

Hexen, die die Kunst verzaubern

Neben dem TV-Material sind das in dem Fall verschiedene Farbfotografien. Sie zeigen die Hexenfamilie bei der Ausübung ihrer Tätigkeit. Uralte Rituale, mit denen sie die Kunst verzaubern. Sie sollen etwa Resonanz und Wirkung beeinflussen: "Dieser Zauber verstärkt die Fähigkeit dieses Kunstwerks, den Betrachter zu bewegen, Emotionen zu wecken und zum Nachdenken anzuregen", steht unter einem der Fotos. Ein anderer verleiht "zusätzliche Kraft, indem er die Karriere und den Status des Künstlers in der Kunstwelt stärkt."

Jankowski werde internationalen Erfolg und Glück haben. Das sei so, wenn Kultur und Magie zusammenkommen, sagt Mihaela Minca. Auf den Bildern sieht man sie und ihre Töchter, samt Objekten und Materialien, die sie für ihre magische Unterstützung brauchen. Gefäße, rote Fäden, Ton, extra dafür geschneiderte Kleider, die ein bisschen an Dolce-und-Gabbana-Entwürfe erinnern.

Schon Mincas Mutter und Großmutter arbeiteten als Hexen. Etwa 1000 rumänische Frauen gibt es, die in diesem Metier tätig sind. Minca bezeichnet sich als die mächtigste von ihnen. Sie berät in Liebesdingen, bei Geldsorgen, Fragen zur Zukunft – und jetzt eben auch in der Kunst. Mit einer Gruppe von anderen Hexen in Los Angeles hat sie mal einen Fluch auf Donald Trump gelegt. Als dieser aber mehr und mehr Ärger auch in seinem Privatleben auslöste, hoben sie den Fluch wieder auf. Die "Vice" berichtete damals .

Hexen-Töchter auf Social Media

Im Fernsehen aber war Minca seit zehn Jahren nicht mehr zu sehen, erzählt ihr Sohn Antonio. Man sei ihrer Kultur dort nicht gerade positiv begegnet, erklärt er weiter. Nur für Jankowskis Kunst habe sie sich nun bereit erklärt, sich filmen zu lassen. Ansonsten überlässt sie das ihren Töchtern, die in schwarzen Kleidern mit langen Schleppen, an denen das ein oder andere Blatt mitgeschleift wird, durch die Ausstellung schweben und in ihre Kameras sprechen. Die Clips werden dann in den sozialen Medien hochgeladen. Magie gebe es, seitdem es Menschen gibt, sagt mir eine der Hexen-Töchter, die so schön und selbstsicher dabei ausschaut, dass man sich natürlich gleich fühlt, als stünde man unter ihrem Einfluss.

Was hier zusammenkommt, sind neue und alte Medien – und mit ihnen Fragen nach Meinungsbildung, Kommunikation, Wahrheit, Glauben und Manipulation. Oder wie es im Ausstellungstext heißt: Der Künstler führe uns zurück "zu der grundlegenden Frage: Wann und wie entsteht der Glaube an eine Idee?"

Er untergrabe so die Funktion der Kunst, der verschiedenen Akteure in der Kunstwelt, die Kategorisierung und die Bewertung von Kunst, heißt es weiter. Aber vielleicht folgt das auch einem überholten Verständnis von Ritual und Religion. Letztere muss ja etwas nicht ersetzen, sondern kann vielmehr ergänzen.

Magie als Kunstvermittlung

Es wirkt jedenfalls nicht so, als würde Jankowski nicht an die Kraft der Kunst glauben und sich deswegen einen Hexenzirkel ins Boot holen. Magie und Ritual werden hier vielmehr zu vollkommen selbstverständlichen und fast notwendigen Praxen der Kunstvermittlung. Wo beginnt eine Idee? Wo beginnt eine Überzeugung? Ein Glaube? Um diese Fragen ginge es ihm, so Jankowski, der diese Ausstellung in nur wenigen Monaten entwickelt hat. Er sagt, er habe ab einem Punkt einfach alles zugelassen und Minca die Entscheidung übergeben.

Und was soll man sagen: Magie als kuratorische Praxis sollte sich durchsetzen. Denn die hier gezeigten Werke passen erstaunlich gut zusammen. Die Arbeit "Seitenwender", eine Palette aus dem Oktober 2025 mit der letzten Ausgabe der gedruckten "Taz", bevor die Tageszeitung nur noch digital erschien. Jankowski hatte die Druckerei besucht und die Hände der dort arbeitenden Menschen fotografiert, die dann auf den Seiten der finalen Papier-"Taz" zu sehen waren.

Am anderen Ende des Raumes wartet die Videoarbeit "Telemistica", die 1999 für die 48. Venedig-Biennale entstand und für die der Künstler fünf TV-Wahrsagerinnen nach der Zukunft und seinem Erfolg bei der weltberühmten Ausstellung befragte. "Magic Numbers" ist ein weiteres Video: 2013 brachte Jankowski dafür Bankangestellte zu Magiern, um Tricks zu lernen, die sie dann bei der Arbeit vorführen konnten. Und auch "The Holy Artwork" von 2001 ist zu sehen. Für den Film begab sich Jankowski zu einer texanischen Kirche, um dort mit einem Fernsehpastor aufzutreten, der für die Kunst Jankowskis betete. All diese Werke fügen sich perfekt in diese Schau ein, die der Kunst das Übersinnliche abverlangt. Und die ihre Macht betont, indem sie sie in Frage stellt.

article_text:
Welcome to The Weekend Read : Deadline’s curated collection of our long-form stories.

We’re mourning one of the greats of stage and screen, Sir Patrick Stewart, who passed away on Wednesday. Read our look back on his beloved work and a collection of remembrances from those who knew him and worked with him.

It’s been a tough week for sad losses, as last Sunday we also said goodbye to much-loved star, Walter Koenig, who originated the role of Ensign Pavel Chekov in the 1960s Star Trek TV series.

We also have some insights from a special AFI Fest screening where audiences were given a brief first-look at The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth , with Quentin Tarantino on hand to discuss.

Take a look at our deep dive into Netflix’s new docuseries The One About Matthew Perry , plus the story of a former Netflix staffer who launched CineYama, a buzzy indie cinema venue in Japan.

And lastly, if you’re wondering what to add to your TV watchlist, we’ve got the rundown on 53 of the hottest new and returning shows of 2026.

Honoring Patrick Stewart — His Obituary & Remembrances From Co-Stars & Friends Image Credit: Tommy Garcia Patrick Stewart , the star of Star Trek: The Next Generation , Star Trek: Picard , the X-Men film franchise and many other movies, TV shows and stage plays, died October 28 at his home in Los Angeles following a battle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. He was 86. A statement from his rep confirmed the news. Stewart, the distinguished stage and screen actor and New York Times best-selling author whose career spanned nearly six decades, was a three-time Olivier Award winner and a Tony Award nominee for his stage work. He won a Grammy in 1995 and received multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations for his work across television and film. In the 2001 New Year Honours list, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE), and in 2010, she knighted for his services to drama. He was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1996. Read the full obituary here. Read a collection of remembrances and tributes here.

Patrick Stewart’s Career In Pictures Sir Patrick Stewart, whose distinctive voice helped him embody everything from USS Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard to the X-Men’s Professor X to Ebenezer Scrooge to an emoji, has died . His decades-long career spans the stage, the big screen, TV and commercials. He worked across genres from sci-fi to Shakespeare, to historical dramas to superhero films to comedy and animation. See the gallery of photos from his career here.

Remembering Walter Koenig — His Obituary And Tributes From ‘Star Trek’s William Shatner & George Takei Image Credit: NBC Walter Koenig , who originated the role of Ensign Pavel Chekov in the 1960s Star Trek TV series and several subsequent movies about the adventures of the USS Enterprise, died Sunday, according to his rep. He was 90. Zachery McGinnis of Galactic Productions posted Monday on Facebook that Koenig died of natural causes in North Hollywood but did not provide other details. “Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen,” McGinnis wrote in part. “Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.” Read the full obituary here. Read William Shatner’s tribute to Koenig here. Read George Takei’s tribute here.

A Brief Look At ‘The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth’ Image Credit: Everett Collection Quentin Tarantino surprised the crowd during a Q&A and screening of his 10-time Oscar-nominated Once Upon a Time in Hollywood on Friday night at AFI Fest in Los Angeles by screening the first 17 minutes of its sequel The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth . It marks the first public look at the film, a follow-up to Hollywood that Tarantino scripted and David Fincher directed. Brad Pitt revisits his Oscar-winning role as Booth, a stuntman and sidekick to Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton in the original 2019 film. Read the full story here.

The One About The Matthew Perry Docuseries – Five Key Takeaways Image Credit: Netflix Let’s be honest, Netflix’s just debuted The One About Matthew Perry is mainly for the hardcore Friends fans. Having said that even the devotees of Rachel, Ross, Monica, Joey, Phoebe and Chandler might be disappointed as there’s not much in this Mary Robertson directed three-part docuseries you haven’t heard before. Over the approximately three-hour running time, The One About draws on tales of drunken nights, funny faces, and the rise, demands, and bends of fame. There’s interviews with old friends, family members (especially Perry’s younger half-sister and licensed therapist Mia Perry Bowick), NBC Entertainment boss Warren Littlefield, The Whole Nine Yards director and one now ex-U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California. Read the full look at the docuseries here.

Japan’s Buzziest New Indie Cinema Venue Image Credit: Matt Kelson. Director Lee Chang-dong’s beautiful genre mash-up, Possible Love ; Dario Argento’s Giallo classic, Suspiria ; and Sophy Romvari’s accomplished debut, Blue Heron , are some of the titles Japanese cinephiles can catch this week at Cineyama , one of the country’s buzziest new indie cinema venues. Located in Yamanashi Prefecture, just outside Tokyo , CineYama is a unique proposition in Japan’s indie film scene: The venue sits at the site of a former kindergarten, and its founder, Matt Kelson, is American. He is also a former senior Netflix staffer. Read the full story here.

53 Of The Hottest New & Returning Shows In 2026 Image Credit: Apple TV 2026 is a big year for TV, and that’s saying something as two of the most popular recent shows — Netflix’s Stranger Things and Prime Video’s The Summer I Turned Pretty — concluded their stories in 2025 (unless the upcoming The Summer I Turned Pretty movie is taken into account, but that is a film and not part of the show). January alone boasted the return of such HBO/HBO Max dramas as The Pitt and Industry and the premiere of Game of Thrones prequel series A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms . And how could we forget the fourth season of Netflix’s Bridgerton — split into two parts again this round — or Season 3 of Apple’s comedy Shrinking ? Read the full list of 53 shows here.

article_text:
写真家・佐々木修宏と増田貴大による二人展「Passings×NOZOMI」part3が、2026年11月20日（金）から23日（月・祝）まで、大阪・十三の済藤美術館で開催される。2024年、2025年に続く第3弾となり、列車の窓越しに捉えた約40点の写真を展示する。

佐々木が発表する「Passings」は、駅のホームから走り去る列車を流し撮りし、窓越しに乗客たちの姿を記録したシリーズ。JR西日本の広告代理店に勤務しながら写真活動を続ける佐々木は、車内で過ごす人々の何気ない仕草や表情を、移動する列車の中から浮かび上がらせる。

一方、増田の「NOZOMI」は、山陽新幹線の車内から沿線の風景や人々を撮影した作品群だ。仕事で新大阪と広島の間を毎日2往復するなか、最高時速300kmで移動する車窓から、一瞬で過ぎ去る光景を流し撮りで捉えてきた。同シリーズは2017年に赤々舎から写真集として刊行され、複数の写真賞でも評価されている。

駅のホームから車内を見つめる佐々木と、車内から外の世界を見つめる増田。視線の方向は正反対でありながら、二人の作品には、窓越しにすれ違う見知らぬ人々との一瞬の出会いを写真にとどめようとする共通点がある。移動する速度と時間のなかに現れる、二度と繰り返されない日常の断片を紹介する展覧会だ。

11月22日（日）18:15からは、写真家で大阪芸術大学教授の吉川直哉を迎え、両作家とのギャラリートークも開催される。

Source: The Bureau Sales / Bankside Films / Global Constellation

‘Black Church Bay’, ‘Surviving Earth’, ‘Straight Circle’

Welsh fishing village drama Black Church Bay , Balkan music story Surviving Earth and political satire Straight Circle lead the British Independent Film Awards (Bifas) new talent filmmaker longlists, with three spots each across the four lists.

Each film is longlisted for breakthrough producer, best debut screenwriter and best debut director; the list for best debut director – feature documentary was also announced.

Scroll down for the full new talent longlists

Black Church Bay writer-director Rhys Marc Jones is listed in the screenwriter and director categories, with Alex Polunin selected in the producer section. Thea Gajic and producer Sophie Reynolds repeat those selections for Surviving Earth ; with Oscar Hudson and producer Rik Green doing likewise for Straight Circle .

Director Molly Manners and screenwriter Miriam Battye are both listed for Extra Geography , as are Samuel Abrahams and Miranda Campbell Bowling, as director and co-writer respectively of Lady .

Louis Paxton is selected in both director and screenwriter categories for debut feature The Incomer . Paxton was selected as a Screen Rising Star Scotland earlier this year.

Other former Screen awardees on the longlists include 2026 Screen UK & Ireland Star of Tomorrow Bertil Nilsson , in writer and director categories for Masc ; 2025 Stars Ted Evans as director of Retreat and Jess O’Kane as writer of Bad Apples ; 2016 Star Billy Lumby as writer and director of Florid ; and Ashley Walters , a Screen Star in the inaugural 2004 edition as an actor, longlisted for best debut director for Animol .

The documentary list includes Ed Sayers for Super Nature and Suki Chan for Conscious .

Longlists for cinema of the year and breakthrough performance were announced earlier this week. Extra Geography , Straight Circle and Surviving Earth lead the way across all lists so far, with four selections each.

The nominees in each category will be announced on Monday, November 3, with the winners revealed at the Bifa ceremony on Sunday, December 6.

article_text:
S cottish Ballet, under the direction of Christopher Hampson and Oscar Sansom, gives us an engrossing dance riff on Shakespeare’s Romeo and Juliet . The title alludes to Friar Lawrence saying, at the couple’s secret wedding ceremony, that “these violent delights have violent ends”, that their passion will consume itself in the act of marriage – which is true, but not in the way he thinks.

The ballet is fierce, athletic, knotty and sensual; it is not a filmed event beneath a proscenium arch but a film that inhabits its own theatrical space. The whole event is a radically impressionistic compression of the play’s action, bringing it down to just 70 minutes, an extended nightmarish dream sequence with a repeated and disturbing scene of Juliet being dragged across the grass by an unseen force. This version chucks out, among other things, the balcony scene, and it interestingly modifies the ending, suggesting that the double-suicide might not be a trick that goes wrong but an anguished mutual gesture of despair.

Intriguingly, it is only really at the end that Romeo (Ishan Mahabir-Stokes) and Juliet (Kayla-Maree Tarantolo) have much time together alone. From the beginning, we see Juliet, frustrated and lonely within her family who are trying to marry her off to the milksop Paris; at one point Paris (Yuri Marques) and Lord Capulet (Christopher Akrill) make her do a bizarre kind of abusive “trust exercise” movement between the two of them. Her nurse (Grace Horler), incidentally, is dressed in the uniform of an NHS-style nurse, as if getting ready to put Juliet in the psych ward if she defies her parents’ wishes.

In her mind, at the outset, she haunts the life of Romeo, as if in a kind of choreographed trance, as he spends parallel time with his family. She has predicted that this is the man who destiny has in store for her. The party scene where they are to meet is held at a club ominously called the Apothecary, and the dance hums with nervous energy and MDMA excitement, but the ballet never permits any simply euphoric private moments of pure love for the star-crossed leads. They are always entangled with other people, vibrating with suspicion, confronting the future that is crowding in on them.

This is a reading of Romeo and Juliet that is all about the alienation of love and the brevity of youth: a dark and pessimistic reading, in its way, but performed with vehement commitment and style.
